How can foods that are not poisonous to us be poisonous to dogs.?

The food that you eat is made up of different chemicals. I don't mean this in the fear-mongering "chemicals are bad" way. We have chemicals inside our body that help us metabolize and digest the food that keeps overall chemical levels in our body within a healthy range that won't kill us. However, different animals have different metabolic ability and some animals just aren't able to handle large amounts of certain chemicals in food that humans can deal with. They can't process the chemical as efficiently as we can, and they're often much smaller than us by body mass so the result is that what we consider a small amount of chocolate might be enough to kill a dog.

(Deviating from ELI5 a bit) For example, you probably know that chocolate is poisonous to dogs. To be specific though, it's theobromine poisoning that actually hurts dogs. In the chart to the right of the linked Wikipedia page, it shows that in order to have a 50% chance of killing a person, that person would need to ingest 1000mg/kg of theobromine; however dogs can only take 300mg/kg before they have a 50/50 chance of dying from it.
Wait.... does that mean it only takes 3ish times as much chocolate to kill a person as a dog (by weight?)

Not a toxicologist, but it seems that way. From the same link I posted above, normal candy chocolate has at most about 2g/kg of theobromine. So you'd have to eat half your body weight of chocolate to have a 50% chance of dying from theobromine.

Normally we'd take a dog to the vet after just a little chocolate so they don't get sick from it rather than to save their life.

Depends on the chocolate. Your dog can eat a hershey bar fine. It'll probably get a tummy ache, but it won't have lasting effect. If it gets into dark chocolate, yeah, you need to get to the vet ASAP before their liver shuts down.

For one example, consider theobromine (a chemical found in chocolate). Theobromine is actually toxic to both humans and dogs, but most of the time we don't have to worry about it for two reasons:

  1. Humans process theobromine much faster than dogs, so it takes a much larger dose/kilo before it starts to seriously affect us.
  2. Humans are much bigger than dogs, which means we have more kilos and require a bigger dose.

There are a lot of reasons why something toxic to one animal might be less toxic to another (otherwise similar) animal. For example, many species have adapted to certain toxins as a result of their diet, and can process them effectively because they have special mechanisms to handle them. In other cases, it may be that one animal uses a particular chemical a certain way, but others do not; delta atracotoxin, for example (used by the funnel web spider) kills primates by interfering with the sodium ion channels in certain neurons, yet has relatively little effect on the (slightly differently structured) channels in many other mammals like cats and dogs.

Thus, there are pretty much three possibilities: either we've evolved specific coping mechanisms, we're immune (or dogs are hypersensitive) due to a quirk of anatomy/neurology, or we may get by simply because we're a lot bigger than dogs and the portions of the toxin we both encounter happen to be enough to kill a dog but not enough to kill a human.

I was taught a variation on Jhyap, or "The Nepalese card game" as he called it, by an American artist living in India. It's a fun quick-fire group game

It's a multi-round trick based game and includes jokers. You'll need to keep a score too. The object of each round is to get your hand down to a value of 5 or less. Aces are worth 1, numbers are worth their number and face cards are 10. Jokers I'll come on to in a moment.

The dealer deals 5 cards to each player, puts the rest of the deck on the table face down, takes the top card and places it face up next to the deck. For this example I'll say that card happened to be the 9 of spades.

The person to the left then has their go. They can discard either a single card or a trick - 2/3/4 of a kind (eg. 7 of hearts + 7 of clubs) or a run of 3 or more of the same suit (eg. 7-8-9 of hearts) onto the face-up card on the table. For the example lets say they played the 7 of hearts and 7 of clubs. They then either pick up the top card from the deck, or the previous card turned over (the 9 of spades).

The next player then plays their hand, and can either pick up any of the discarded cards from the turn before (7 of hearts and 7 of clubs) or take from the top of the deck.

By playing tricks you discard more than you pick up, so the number of cards in your hand slowly goes down making it easier to reduce the value to 5 or less.

If you don't have a trick you just put down a single card and pick another up. Often you'll find that picking one of the cards played in the turn before will make a trick for your next turn, otherwise you'll just have to pick from the deck and hope it matches something.

If you get through all the cards in the deck you shuffle the discarded cards, place them face down in the middle again and place the top card face up next to the deck and carry on.

Once the total value of your hand at the start of your turn is 5 or less then you can "call" that round (you can only call at the start of your go, not after you've discarded). After you call all the other players have to show their hand. The value of their hand is added to their score (lower is better) while the person calling gets no points for their hand. However if someone else has a score the same or lower than the calling player the calling player gets a 25 point penalty. You don't have to call even if your hand is 5 or less, so if you think someone else might have a lower score it's best to just play a card normally instead of calling.

The person who called is then the dealer, all the cards are collected, the deck is shuffled and a new round begins. There are several ways you can "end" a game, either stop once any player goes over 100 points (at which point the player with the lowest score win) or you can play where every time a player goes over 100 they are out, and you play until there's only 1 player left.

Now for jokers, during the game they act as a wildcard so you can use them as any part of a trick (eg. 4-joker-6-7 of hearts, or 1-2-3-4 of a kind + joker). When calling they are worth 1 point (same as aces) but if someone else calls and you have a joker in your hand they are worth 40 points (so use carefully)

Finally to keep things moving round the table quickly there's the "slap" rule. When taking from the top of the deck if the card you picked up would have made a trick with the cards you just played you can discard it ("slap it down") if the next player hasn't had their turn yet. For example if you played the 7 of diamonds and picked up the 7 of hearts from the deck you can slap it straight down, or if you played the 6-7-8 of clubs and picked the 5 of clubs up, or if it's a joker.

Because of that other players should have their move ready so as soon as the player before picks a card from the top of the deck they can play their cards into the discard pile to prevent the previous player from slapping. If a player is left with no cards after a slap (i.e. they slapped their last card) then they automatically win that round and the points of everyone elses' hands are totalled as per if a player called.

Finally for big groups you can shuffle 2 decks together to make sure there are enough cards to keep it fluid.

Egyptian Rat Screw, or ERS. This game works much better the more players you have, as the object is to collect the entire deck.

  1. Deal entire deck to all players. (All players must keep their cards face down.)
  2. The dealer flips their top card away from himself and places it face up in the center of the table.
  3. The player to his left quickly does the same, and so on and so forth.
  4. Upon two of the same card being placed down in a row ( two fours ), or a "sandwich" ( four, six, four ), any player may slap the deck to claim all cards that have been played so far as their own.
  5. If multiple slap at once, the player who contacted the deck first, or is on the bottom of the pile of hands gets the cards.
  6. Play resumes with the player who took the deck.
  7. If only one player has cards in their hand (and hasn't won all of them, for example if other players ran out while placing), they continue to quickly place down cards until they can claim the pile...or someone else does.
